content_voiceover: Burkitt lymphoma is the single most aggressive B cell lymphoma, but also one of the most curable when treated correctly. Nearly one hundred percent of cells are Ki-67 positive, reflecting an extremely high proliferation rate. The defining molecular lesion is c-MYC overexpression, most commonly from the t 8;14 translocation involving the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, seen in about eighty percent of cases, with the remainder driven by light chain partners, t 2;8 with kappa or t 8;22 with lambda. The typical immunophenotype is surface immunoglobulin positive, CD10 positive, CD20 positive, TdT negative, Ki-67 positive at ninety-five percent or higher, BCL2 negative, and BCL6 positive. Cytogenetically it's usually a simple karyotype with the MYC rearrangement as the sole abnormality, which helps distinguish it from double-hit lymphomas. There are three clinical subtypes: endemic, sporadic, and HIV-related. Clinically, expect a bulky abdominal mass, B symptoms, and bone marrow involvement in about seventy percent of cases. The endemic African form classically presents with a jaw or facial mass in children.
keypoints: Most aggressive B-cell lymphoma; Ki-67 near 100%
MYC-driven: t(8;14) IGH in 80%; light chain variants t(2;8), t(8;22)
Immunophenotype: CD10+, CD20+, BCL2-, BCL6+, TdT-; simple karyotype
Endemic (jaw mass), sporadic, and HIV-related subtypes
